title: Let Freedom Ring
author: Becky Abrams Wilmoth
summary: In this guest post for Restarting School, Becky Abrams Wilmoth draws a parallel between America's founding freedoms and the freedom parents lack to choose where their children are educated. She traces the progress of school choice legislation — including the 2025 Universal School Choice Act introduced by Ted Cruz and a federal Individual Tax Credit for Scholarship Granting Organizations — noting that 31 states have opted in while governors in Minnesota, Wisconsin, New Mexico, and Oregon have refused. Oregon is the article's primary case study in failure: last among 50 states in 4th-grade reading scores (adjusted for demographics) and 49th in 8th-grade math, yet blocking families from accessing alternatives. Wilmoth argues that parents' inability to direct their education dollars is incompatible with a free country's values and outlines three pathways for advocates in non-ESA states: state legislative engagement, affordable microschool development, and church-based scholarship networks.
points: Americans are free to choose their bank, neighborhood, and college — but in most states, children cannot use their portion of public education funding to attend a school that meets their individual needs.

The 2025 Universal School Choice Act and the federal Individual Tax Credit for Scholarship Granting Organizations have created a federal pathway for school choice, but 31 states have opted in while several blue-state governors have blocked access.

Oregon ranks last among 50 states in 4th-grade reading scores adjusted for demographics and 49th in 8th-grade math — yet the governor has blocked the federal school choice program that could fund alternatives.

Private school tuition in Southern Oregon ranges from $11,000–$20,000 per student per year at the elementary level and $13,000–$23,000 at the middle/high level — effectively prohibitive for middle-class families with multiple children.

Advocates in non-ESA states have three pathways: state legislative engagement, developing affordable hybrid and microschool options, and building church networks to provide private scholarship funding.
quotes: We are free to choose where we bank, where we live, where to attend college. Why are our children not free to attend the school that they choose?

School choice is the civil rights issue of the 21st century. Every child in America deserves access to a quality education that meets their individual needs, regardless of race, ethnicity, income, or zip code.

Oregon comes in last among the 50 states for fourth grade reading scores, adjusted for demographics, according to the Urban Institute, and 49th for eighth grade math. One in three students is chronically absent
Advocating for school choice in blue states requires a multifaceted approach that blends policy creativity, strategic messaging, and coalition-building
Children should be able to learn in environments that fit their needs. Parents should be able to choose that environment without the financial barriers so many families currently face.
